newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Lloyd's must scrap annual venture - CLM chief exec.
newsitem.headline: Lloyd's must scrap annual venture - CLM chief exec.

text.p: Corporate investors could flood into Lloyd's of London and push its capacity to 15 billion pounds, but only if it scraps its annual venture system, a senior market figure said on Wednesday.

"The Lloyd's market will be in a position to meet future challenges provided that it moves rapidly away from the annual joint venture towards a market place that will embrace insurance companies," Michael Wade, chief executive of Lloyd's corporate capital vehicle CLM Insurance Fund, told a conference in Dublin.

Speaking the day after news that Commercial Union was to become the latest insurance company to invest at Lloyd's, Wade said: "It is possible to foresee a market with a 15 billion (pounds) premium capacity with trading companies as large as one billion pounds and as small as 10 million pounds."

Capital providers at Lloyd's band together to form a syndicate for a calendar year and employ an underwriter to accept risks on their behalf. A syndicate runs for an accounting period of 36 months, after which profits are paid out.
However, as British government rules say no reserves can be transferred forward, the syndicate has to be reconstituted each year to take on new risks.

Syndicates are therefore operated by managing agents with a direct interest in the profitability of the company, but no liability for losses. The syndicate is not a legal entity and therefore not the insurance vehicle.

"The whole vulnerability of this extraordinary structure became exposed during the Reconstruction and Renewal period. It is wrong to continue with it," Wade told delegates at the London International Insurance and Reinsurance Market Association (LIRMA) seminar in Dublin.
Wade said the system made it difficult to accept long term contracts that embrace customers' needs. But, more importantly, he spelled out the high costs involved in maintaining the annual system.

"The need to employ large numbers of people to negotiate each year the size of a particular business and put the arrangements in place is an appalling waste of resources and one which you will not find mirrored anywhere else in the world," he said.
"There is a huge hidden expense because the requirement of investment policy prescribes that this can only be committed to cash or very short, non-volatile forms of investment," he added.
Wade said that to obtain licenses in the U.S., American Trust Funds have to be formed as a bond to policyholders which require restructuring for each annual venture.
"The clumsiness of their impact reaches the point where it actually puts into question whether it is viable to trade in the U.S. at all under the current structure," Wade said.
Finally, he highlighted the cost of regulating the system in the UK.
"Can you imagine how much all this costs as compared with capital provided to insurance companies by the shareholders as opposed to traders?" he said.

Corporate capital now represents 44 percent of Lloyd's, with the remainder coming from individual investors known in the market as Names. The figure has risen sharply since corporate capital was introduced in 1994, and many market observers believe it will soon become the dominant force.

"The structural framework needs to evolve whereby the managing agency and the capital provider are brought together by forming a company to replace the managed syndicate arrangement with disparate capital and insuring units," Wade said.
"Let us be in no doubt that there would be great danger in delaying this process for a moment longer than is necessary. We should aim to complete this process in three years," he said.
